title: PhysInfer: A physics-constrained neural network for adaptive inference of transcriptional bursting from single-cell RNA-seq
text: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has established that gene expression is driven by stochastic transcriptional bursting. However, inferring burst dynamics from static scRNA-seq snapshots is fundamentally constrained by parameter unidentifiability and model topology mismatch. Here, we propose PhysInfer, an unsupervised framework that integrates a physics-constrained neural network with adaptive model selection and parameter decoupling. A physics-informed loss function, combining stationary-distribution likelihood with zero-count anchoring, reparameterizes the optimization from unidentifiable microscopic rates to an interpretable macroscopic burst-quantity representation of burst size and burst frequency, thereby providing an interpretable parameterization for assessing practical recoverability in static data. Validation on synthetic data with known ground-truth parameters confirms high inference accuracy in low-to-medium activation regimes and shows that recovery of BS and productive BF becomes increasingly condition-dependent as the ON-state probability approaches saturation; under different recovery criteria, the condition-specific upper Pon limit for simultaneously recovering BS and productive BF varies with cell number and capture efficiency. Applied to a mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) dataset, PhysInfer reconstructs a transcriptional dynamic manifold across the 2,137-gene secondary BIC analysis set, showing cross-gene variation in fitted burst frequency and burst size. A model-specific stationary likelihood combined with zero-count anchoring improves robustness to zero-heavy observations. The adaptive topology module further identifies a distinct subset of genes with stable support for an effective sequential 3-state representation, revealing distributional structure beyond that captured by standard 2-state fitting. PhysInfer thus provides a robust, topology-adaptive, and interpretable solution for characterizing transcriptional kinetic patterns from static single-cell transcriptomic snapshots.

title: Expanded repeat RNAs drive aberrant cortical network activity in benign adult familial myoclonus epilepsy.
text: Expansions of short nucleotide repeats cause diverse neurological disorders, yet how they perturb neuronal function remains unclear. Benign adult familial myoclonus epilepsy (BAFME) is caused by intronic pentanucleotide repeat expansions in genes including SAMD12. Here, we establish patient-derived cortical organoids and a microelectrode array platform, coupled with a frequency-decomposition-based analytical framework, to characterize BAFME-associated neuronal hyperexcitability and compare organoid electrophysiological features with those observed in patient electroencephalographic recordings. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals altered expression of genes related to calcium regulation and α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptor function in BAFME cortical neurons. Consistent with these changes, BAFME organoids show an increased density of AMPA-receptor-positive synaptic puncta. Pharmacological AMPA receptor antagonism suppresses hyperexcitability. Antisense oligonucleotides targeting the expanded repeat RNA-which reduce pathogenic RNA foci without significantly affecting SAMD12 mRNA levels-also attenuate hyperexcitability. These findings indicate that targeting expanded repeat RNA mitigates aberrant cortical network activity in BAFME organoids.

title: Application of AI-designed OpenCRISPR-1 for highly efficient gene editing in soybean (Glycine max L.) and Nicotiana benthamiana.
text: The widespread application of CRISPR/Cas genome editing for commercial crop improvement is currently hindered by a complex and restrictive intellectual property (IP) landscape. The recent development of OpenCRISPR-1, a fully AI-designed Cas9-like nuclease, provides a promising alternative with an accessible licensing framework; however, its efficacy in dicotyledonous plants remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we report the successful adaptation of the OpenCRISPR-1 system for targeted mutagenesis in soybean (Glycine max L.) and Nicotiana benthamiana. We constructed a plant-optimized binary vector (pBSE-OpenCRISPR-1) and validated its editing capability. In soybean (Glycine max), an Agrobacterium rhizogenes-mediated hairy root transformation assay targeting the GmFAD2-1B gene demonstrated that OpenCRISPR-1 actively induces site-specific mutations. In Nicotiana benthamiana, stable Agrobacterium-mediated transformation targeting the phytoene desaturase homologs (NbPDSa/b) achieved overall editing in 75% of T0 transgenic lines (27/36). Analysis of individual homologs revealed editing rates of 66.7% (24/36) at both the NbPDSa and NbPDSb loci. Complete editing of the target locus occurred in 13.9% of events for NbPDSb and 2.8% for NbPDSa, including one event (2.8%) displaying simultaneous complete editing across all alleles resulting in a visible albino phenotype. Deep amplicon and Sanger sequencing revealed a characteristic mutation profile dominated by small insertions and deletions occurring two to three nucleotides upstream of the PAM. These results demonstrate that the AI-designed OpenCRISPR-1 system is a highly active and versatile nuclease for dicot genome engineering. By providing expanded freedom-to-operate, this tool broadens access to crop trait improvement worldwide.

title: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Palindromic Repeats-Cas Genome-Editing Systems in Filamentous Fungi: Current Tools, Optimization Strategies, and Future Perspectives.
text: Filamentous fungi are important microbial cell factories for producing antibiotics, organic acids, enzymes, and other valuable products, with broad applications in food, agriculture, and medicine. However, inefficient and imprecise genome editing remains a major bottleneck limiting rational strain engineering. This review summarizes major genome-editing tools in filamentous fungi, including Cre-loxP, TALENs, and CRISPR-Cas systems, with emphasis on their mechanisms, advantages, and limitations. We highlight CRISPR-Cas9 as the predominant platform and discuss optimization strategies involving sgRNA design, engineered Cas9 variants, promoter engineering, AMA1-based replicative plasmids, and ribonucleoprotein delivery. Emerging technologies, including base editing, prime editing, Cas12a, and Mad7, are also discussed for their potential to broaden editing capabilities. Finally, we outline future perspectives focusing on extending the application of existing genome-editing systems in filamentous fungi and discovering novel genome-editing tools from large-scale omics data sets. This review will accelerate the development of filamentous fungi as versatile platforms for biomanufacturing.

title: Liver immune tolerance and regulated cell death in transplantation and hepatocellular carcinoma: shared mechanisms, divergent outcomes.
text: The liver constantly encounters gut-derived antigens, microbial molecules, and food antigens. This environment has shaped a tissue-specific tolerance network centered on tolerogenic antigen presentation, immune-checkpoint activation, regulatory cell expansion, and metabolic suppression. This feature protects the liver during prolonged inflammation and gives it an immunological identity that most solid organs lack. Regulated cell death (RCD) and dead-cell clearance form a critical mechanistic layer within this network. Efficient efferocytosis of apoptotic cells reinforces resolution and tolerance, whereas necroptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis disrupt cell membranes and release danger signals that reshape myeloid activation, T-cell function, and the tumor microenvironment. In liver transplantation, this tolerogenic tendency produces donor-specific hyporesponsiveness, allowing a selected subset of stable recipients to stop immunosuppression while maintaining graft function-a state called operational tolerance. In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), tumors exploit the same immunosuppressive axes to block anti-tumor T-cell infiltration and effector function. Anti-PD-L1 therapy combined with anti-angiogenic treatment improves survival, demonstrating that partial disruption of tumor immunosuppression is therapeutically effective. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell sequencing reveal that SPP1-positive macrophages and cancer-associated fibroblasts form a tumor immune barrier that excludes lymphocytes, showing that hepatic tolerance is organized in space. This duality becomes most dangerous in HCC recurrence after liver transplantation, where immune checkpoint inhibitors boost anti-tumor immunity but also raise the risk of acute rejection, graft failure, and death. Unlike reviews focused on hepatic immune tolerance, regulated cell death, or HCC immunobiology in isolation, this review integrates these processes across the physiological liver, transplantation, HCC, and post-transplant recurrence. We define this coordinated hyporesponsive state as the liver immune tolerance program (ITP), generated by cellular, molecular, spatial, metabolic, and cell-death-related networks. Rather than treating these processes separately, we position RCD and dead-cell clearance as a "death-to-immunity axis," systematically compare ITP remodeling in the physiological liver, transplantation, and HCC, and use post-transplant HCC recurrence as a clinical crossover setting in which graft protection and antitumor immune surveillance become therapeutic considerations. On this basis, we propose precision immune homeostasis: rather than choosing between immunosuppression and immune activation, immune status should be adjusted to an individualized range that protects the graft while preserving anti-tumor immune surveillance.

title: Spatial Niches Shape Function in the Intratumoral Microbiome: From Multiscale Mapping to Niche-Informed Therapy.
text: Most studies of the intratumoral microbiome describe microbial composition and abundance but do not reveal where bacteria are located within the tumor microenvironment. Evidence that microbial signals vary across tumor regions and host-cell compartments makes spatial context essential to biological interpretation. In this review, we organize evidence at three levels: tissue niches reflect oxygenation, perfusion, pH, necrosis, and anatomy, cellular niches involve malignant, immune, and stromal cells, and physical interfaces include intracellular residence, extracellular association, biofilms, and diffusible products. We examine how contamination-aware sequencing, single-cell host-microbe profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and imaging distinguish detection from localization and relate microbial geography to host-cell states. Spatial organization may affect oncogenic signaling, cytoskeletal remodeling, DNA damage, immune regulation, metastatic fitness, and treatment response. The same bacterial strain may exert opposing immune effects inside and outside host cells. This framework clarifies therapeutic implications. Engineered bacteria can deliver payloads to hypoxic, poorly perfused regions, whereas intracellular nanocarriers, species-selective phages, and biofilm-disrupting platforms address different microbial reservoirs. Major limitations include low-biomass contamination, uncertain viability, incomplete localization, limited causal evidence, and poorly resolved temporal dynamics. Integrating microbial identity with location and physical state should yield more mechanistic models of the intratumoral microbiome and better-defined therapeutic strategies.

title: Population-scale integration of spatial omics networks for clinical prediction and biological discovery by SPIN.
text: Spatial omics enables the integration of high-dimensional molecular organization with clinical outcomes, yet incorporating spatial single-cell information into predictive models at the population scale remains challenging. We introduce SPIN (spatial predictive integration network), which integrates subject-specific, cell-type level, spatially informed co-expression or co-abundance networks for population-scale clinical prediction. Current implementation of SPIN includes three key modules: network construction, molecular-to-clinical prediction by Bayesian scalar-on-network regression with manifold learning (BSNMani), and visualization & interpretation module. In the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD) multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) transcriptomics cohort, SPIN achieved an accuracy of 0.81 for dementia-status prediction and revealed co-expression subnetworks with clear biological relevance. SPIN also achieved robust survival prediction in a breast cancer single-cell proteomics cohort (C-index = 0.78), identifying two survival-associated spatial proteomic subnetworks. In summary, SPIN is an interpretable tool for spatial-omics-based clinical outcome prediction at the population scale.

title: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia.
text: Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain. This study delineates the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and single-molecule chromatin + RNA imaging, and we found heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions. Spiny projection neurons (SPNs), the principal cells of the BG, acquire distinct subtypes through synchronized 3D-epigenomic remodeling, in contrast to the asynchronous maturation of other neuron types. Oligodendrocyte differentiation involves a transient short-range chromatin state during infancy, showing that the short-range and long-range chromatin conformations previously linked to terminal glial and neuronal fates can also be transient. The temporal cortex matured epigenomically faster than other cortical regions during this period. Lastly, SPNs were enriched in genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study extends findings on unique 3D-epigenomic dynamics during human brain development.

title: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain.
text: Direct measurement of chromatin states together with transcription is essential for understanding how cell-type-specific regulatory programs are established and maintained in the adult human brain. Here, we present a large-scale single-cell multimodal atlas by jointly profiling the transcriptome with active (H3K27ac) or repressive (H3K27me3) histone modifications across 18 adult brain regions. We targeted over 750,000 nuclei spanning 160 cell types and integrated these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, 3D genome architecture, and spatial transcriptomes. This framework resolved chromatin states for over 500,000 candidate regulatory elements, identified enhancer-gene links and regulatory programs, revealed Polycomb-associated ultra-long-range contacts, and uncovered brainwide epigenomic heterogeneity. We further developed a sequence-to-function model to predict cell-type-specific effects of candidate neurological disease variants. Finally, comparative analyses across species reveal conservation in active regulatory programs but divergence in repressive programs. Together, this study provides a comprehensive epigenomic reference for interpreting regulatory principles and epigenetic memory underlying human brain organization and disease.

title: The surgeon in the loop: automation bias and human-AI interaction in robotic surgery.
text: Artificial intelligence systems for intraoperative surgical guidance are approaching clinical deployment, yet no study has quantified automation bias (defined as the tendency to over-rely on automated recommendations) in the context of surgical decision-making. As these systems enter operative workflows, the surgeon's ability to recognize and override incorrect AI guidance becomes a critical safety requirement. To measure the extent to which surgeons modify incision plans after exposure to AI-labeled visual guidance and to determine the rate at which incorrect AI suggestions are accepted. A two-phase controlled experiment was conducted among 19 surgeons (10 residents, 2 fellows, 7 attendings). Participants drew incision lines on 20 static frames from robotic cholecystectomy videos, first without guidance (Phase 01) and then with a mock AI overlay (Phase 02). Overlays were either correct (derived from expert consensus) or deliberately incorrect (shifted toward unsafe anatomy) at an approximately 70:30 ratio. No actual AI model was used. The primary outcome was mean perpendicular distance (MPD) between Phase 01 and Phase 02 lines. Secondary outcomes included AI-corridor adherence, over-reliance and under-reliance rates, behavioral accuracy, and confidence shift. Across 231 paired observations, MPD did not differ significantly between correct (75.5 pixels; SD, 33.4) and incorrect (71.1 pixels; SD, 31.7) overlay conditions (P = .35). Directional analysis revealed that surgeons accepted incorrect AI suggestions in 60.6% of incorrect-overlay frames (43/71), with a specificity for rejecting incorrect guidance of only 39.4% (28/71). Correct suggestions were accepted 76.9% of the time (123/160). Overall behavioral accuracy was 65.4%. Self-reported confidence increased significantly after AI exposure (Δ = + 0.65; P < .001). Surgeons accepted approximately 3 of every 5 incorrect AI recommendations. As intraoperative AI systems approach deployment, surgeon oversight cannot be assumed to neutralize algorithmic error; it must be empirically measured, deliberately designed for, and prospectively validated.

title: Fluid-driven robotic micromanipulation for assembloid fabrication.
text: The assembly of cellular spheroids into spatially organized assembloids represents a transformative paradigm for modeling complex biological systems. However, the lack of standardized fabrication strategies fundamentally limits the precision and reproducibility of these models, hindering their widespread application. Here, we present a robotic micromanipulation platform-Fluid-Driven Tweezer with Visual Servo Control (FDT-VSC). By integrating multidimensional visual perception with microfluidic control, our system enables the gentle and programmable assembly of diverse cellular spheroids. Leveraging this platform, we achieve the bottom-up construction of structurally defined, heterogeneous multicellular tissues, and the programmed orchestration of multilineage models that recapitulate the complex microenvironments of early organogenesis. Crucially, the system improves consistency during the scalable fabrication of tumor-stroma assembloids, supporting reliable drug screening. These results demonstrate that FDT-VSC advances assembloid-based applications across modular tissue engineering, developmental biology, and drug discovery.

title: Streamline CNV - A Handy Nextflow Pipeline for Chromosomal Copy Number Variation Analysis.
text: Aneuploidy, characterized by imbalanced chromosomal copy number variation (CNV), occurs in both normal somatic tissues and a wide range of diseases. Low pass whole genome sequencing (LP-WGS) to detect CNVs in cells and tissues has been widely used in all biological research. Existing informatics tools for detecting CNV often require computational expertise, often posing challenges for wet-lab biologists. To address this need, we developed Streamline CNV (SLCNV) - a user-friendly and flexible copy number analysis pipeline that allows researchers to perform many copy number-related analyses steps with a single, straightforward command. Streamline CNV is based on Nextflow and is packaged in a Docker image that can be executed using Singularity, making it portable and reproducible across different user environments. The pipeline automatically processes input data, performs sequencing quality control to filter problematic samples, outputs mapping statistics, CNV calling, and generates outputs including intuitive CNV plots, segmentation files (with statistics), annotation of genes on altered chromosomes, evaluation of proportion of chromosomal regions that are non-euploid. Based on user preferences, it can cluster samples solely based on CNV patterns, map the genomic location and density of genes of interest along chromosomes, and visually highlight regions with evident CNVs. In addition, it allows users to select and order chromosomes for display in plots, define sample label color palettes, and choose whether to include sample labels in the clustering visualizations. It also allows users to specify the amount of computing resources to allocate to the pipeline, such as CPU, memory, and runtime. Streamline CNV can be customizable and upgradable. It works with any species and genome assembly and efficiently supports both single-cell and bulk sequencing data with improved performance coding. Jobs can be distributed across cores of a basic Unix workstation, multiple nodes in a high-performance computing cluster using the Slurm scheduler, or cloud environments, as needed. We demonstrated the tool using an in-house sequencing dataset of human and mouse cell lines. Our results showed that the Streamline CNV pipeline effectively detected copy number patterns and generated informative summaries. It annotated the findings by identifying affected genes within the copy-number segments and at the break-end regions. It also reported the proportions of altered chromosomal regions impacted by copy number changes for each sample. The clustering plot demonstrated the relationships between samples based on their copy number profiles. Gene density plots aid in interpreting how genes from distinct pathways are associated with CNV pattern alterations. This tool enables researchers, regardless of bioinformatics expertise, to perform comprehensive CNV analyses across a wide range of scenarios. It also facilitates the interpretation of the copy number results and makes it possible for transforming raw CNV data into further exploration of meaningful biological insights.

title: Allogeneic CAR-T, CAR-NK, and in vivo CAR-T for immune-mediated inflammatory diseases: comparative evidence, platform trade-offs, and translational challenges.
text: Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) remain treatment-dependent in many patients with severe, refractory, or organ-threatening disease. Deep B-cell depletion using chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based therapies may induce clinical improvement and measurable immune reconstitution, but conventional autologous CAR-T manufacturing limits speed, standardization, and access. This structured narrative review compares allogeneic CAR-T, allogeneic CAR-natural killer (CAR-NK), and in vivo CAR-T. Bibliographic databases, trial registries, conference repositories, reference lists, and traceable sponsor, media, and regulatory sources were searched through 3 September 2026. Allogeneic CAR-T has the broadest clinical evidence base, although cohorts are small and mostly early-phase. All CAR-NK products with reported IMID clinical data are allogeneic; available studies suggest transient kinetics, repeat-infusion feasibility, and encouraging short-term tolerability, but durability is uncertain. Peer-reviewed in vivo evidence now includes a five-patient non-integrating LNP/linear mRNA report and a 16-patient integrating lentiviral report. Both are early, uncontrolled studies and neither supports class-wide inference. Disease-specific outcomes, background treatment, follow-up, and assays differ markedly. Complete treatment-free remission was distinguished from glucocorticoid withdrawal, immunosuppressant reduction, and remission on permitted therapy. CAR-cell, transgene DNA, and RNA detection were not pooled, and peripheral blood B-cell depletion was not treated as proof of tissue depletion. Naive-dominant B-cell recovery and declining autoantibodies indicate immune remodeling, not restored tolerance. No indirect efficacy ranking is justified. Prospective studies need standardized disease endpoints, treatment-free remission definitions, analyte-specific pharmacokinetics, paired blood-tissue pharmacodynamics, and long-term genomic, immune, and safety surveillance.

title: BIOREDIS: an integrated platform for end-to-end design of nucleic acid therapeutics.
text: Developing state-of-the-art RNA- and DNA-based therapeutics requires advanced computational frameworks that support the entire workflow - from biological rationale to the final drug construct - enabling tissue- and cell-specific targeting with high precision. Existing bioinformatics tools provide only partial solutions and rarely generate designs directly suitable for synthesis or preclinical evaluation. To address these limitations, we present BIOREDIS, a web-based platform for comprehensive nucleic acid therapeutic design. BIOREDIS integrates curated data from nine major biological resources and incorporates modules for coding sequence optimization, RNA interference (shRNA/siRNA) design, promoter/UTR selection, and automated construction of viral (AAV, lentiviral), non-viral, and mRNA vaccine vectors. The platform supports designs for human, mouse, and rat, with tissue-specific promoter recommendations available for human and mouse, and advanced cell-expression profiling natively restricted to human. BIOREDIS demonstrates competitive performance in coding sequence optimization and RNAi prediction, while uniquely providing an end-to-end workflow from target selection to fully specified next-generation DNA or RNA therapeutic constructs ready for synthesis and experimental validation. BIOREDIS is freely available at https://rnadrug.ichb.pl/bioredis, with a mirror site at https://bioredis.cs.put.poznan.pl. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Causal Machine Learning for Treatment Effect Heterogeneity: Interpretation, Benchmarking, Validation.
text: Causal machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising approach for predicting individualized treatment effects and advancing precision medicine, moving beyond the limitations of conventional one-variable-at-a-time subgroup analyses of randomized trials. A recent benchmarking study by Chen and colleagues evaluated several causal ML learners across two large trials and concluded that current methods do not yet demonstrate reliable performance for clinical application. While such applied methodological investigations are valuable, this conclusion warrants a more nuanced examination. Multiple independent research groups have successfully applied causal ML across respiratory medicine and critical care, identifying clinically meaningful treatment effect heterogeneity that prior subgroup analyses had not resolved, although these applications have methodological limitations and do not yet establish that the detected heterogeneity is robust across internal and external validation. We outline four sequential and iterative dimensions central to credible causal ML analyses: choice of learner, model training with cross-fitting, internal validation using calibration-for-benefit and rank-weighted metrics, and external validation aligned with the original causal question. With careful methodological execution, causal ML holds considerable promise for personalized treatment decisions and warrants continued development; dismissing the field prematurely risks overlooking a powerful tool for personalized treatment decisions.

title: Luenberger observers for two-gene regulatory networks with sigmoidal regulation: explicit observability conditioning, polytopic convergence certificates, and a logistic--Hill comparison
text: Only a few species of a gene regulatory network can be measured, so the others must be reconstructed by a state observer, and how well this works depends on the function chosen to describe regulation. We examine this for the two-gene negative feedback loop with one measured protein, for monotone regulation functions including the logistic function and the Hill function with its leaky and shifted variants. Using standard tools, we show that the answer is set by the smallest and the largest slope of the regulation function on the concentrations visited. For every function considered, the unmeasured concentration can be recovered from the measured signal and its rate of change, with an error sensitivity set by the smallest slope. A Luenberger observer with explicit gains converges exponentially from any initial guess and tolerates bounded measurement noise whenever a checkable matrix condition involving only the largest slope holds, as it does for every model examined with bounded slopes. The guaranteed rate cannot exceed the degradation rate of the unmeasured protein unless the smallest slope is positive, and faster rates then hold only for small initial errors. All reported rates are certified from above and below. At matched threshold and steepness, no family is uniformly better: the logistic function is better conditioned when the threshold lies mid-range, leaky or shifted Hill functions when it lies low. Hill functions with exponent below one have an unbounded slope at zero concentration and lose the global guarantee, which logistic and shifted Hill functions keep.

title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
text: Abstract Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment 1–8 , suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear 9–13 . Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

title: AmpliconSuite: an end-to-end workflow for analyzing focal amplifications in cancer genomes
text: Abstract Here we present AmpliconSuite, a toolkit for focal amplification analysis from cancer whole-genome sequencing that identifies extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), breakage–fusion–bridges and other amplification modes. Its ecContext module categorizes ecDNA structures to understand formation mechanisms. Validation across 175 metaphase fluorescence in situ hybridization-probed genes in 72 models demonstrated accurate predictions. Analysis of 6,506 patient pan-cancer samples revealed ecDNA-mediated oncogene co-amplification preferences. To democratize data sharing, we created AmpliconRepository, a community-contributable platform, enabling investigation of results across >15,000 publicly hosted samples.

title: A Prospective Trial of SFI Plus PD-1 Inhibitors and PBC in Resectable NSCLC (SFI-NSCLC)
text: [Fase: PHASE4; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This prospective, single-center clinical trial will enroll 30 treatment-naïve patients with locally advanced, resectable stage II-IIIA non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) to receive neoadjuvant Shenqi Fuzheng Injection (SFI) in combination with a PD-1 inhibitor and platinum-based chemotherapy. The primary endpoint is the pathological complete response (pCR) rate, while secondary endpoints include the major pathological response (MPR) rate and event-free survival (EFS). Furthermore, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics will be employed to dynamically track alterations in the immune regulatory network within the tumor microenvironment (TME) pre- and post-SFI administration. This approach aims to elucidate how SFI remodels the TME immune landscape and to uncover its potential advantages in improving clinical outcomes. Additionally, we will investigate the synergistic effects of SFI combined with PD-1 blockade and platinum-based chemotherapy, with the ultimate goal of advancing the integration of traditional Chinese medicine into the therapeutic paradigm for resectable NSCLC.

title: WHO guidance helps detect iron deficiency and protect brain development
text: Detecting iron deficiency early during pregnancy and in young children is crucial. Iron deficiency in children under two years of age can have significant and irreversible effects on brain development. This can lead to negative consequences on learning and school performance later in life. Cognitive development of a child can also be affected if a mother is iron deficient during her last trimester of pregnancy. New World Health Organization guidelines on the use of ferritin concentrations to assess iron status in individuals and populations will help health workers to detect iron deficiency early and avoid the most severe impacts.  WHO shows how to best measure ferritin, an indicator of iron stores, to help determine iron deficiency or overload. Ferritin is a protein which can be found in small amounts circulating in a person’s blood. Ferritin levels are low in iron-deficient individuals and high in iron-loaded individuals. Accurate measurements of this protein, along with clinical and laboratory evaluation, can guide the appropriate interventions in both individual patients and at a population level. “Reducing anemia is one of the components of our efforts to eradicate all forms of malnutrition. However, progress has been limited and we still have 614 million women and 280 million children globally who suffer from it,” said Dr Francesco Branca, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety at WHO. “Iron deficiency is a major determinant of anemia and measuring ferritin, a key biomarker of iron metabolism, will help us better target and evaluate our action to fight anemia” Iron is an essential element with important functions such as oxygen transport, DNA synthesis and muscle metabolism. Iron deficiency is the main cause of anaemia, which is the most prevalent nutritional deficiency worldwide, affecting 33% of non-pregnant women, 40% of pregnant women, and 42% of children worldwide. In adults, iron deficiency can also have negative effects including fatigue, impaired physical performance and decreased work productivity, as well as impacting social activities. Iron deficiency occurs mainly when the requirements of iron increase during rapid periods of growth and development such as in early childhood, adolescence and pregnancy, but it can occur at other stages in life. In pregnant women, iron deficiency can cause anaemia, reduced birth weight and reduced gestation periods. The new guidelines also cover the early detection of iron overload. Iron overload (accumulation of iron in the body) is generally the result of disorders such as hereditary haemochromatosis, thalassaemia, repeated blood transfusions or other conditions that affect iron absorption or regulation and can also lead to deterioration of a person’s health if left untreated. Improved knowledge about the prevalence and distribution of iron deficiency and risk of iron overload in the population helps countries to decide on appropriate interventions, and to monitor and evaluate the impact and safety of public health programmes. For example, nutritional iron deficiency can be commonly found in populations that also have infectious diseases. The adequate evaluation of iron status in countries with infectious disorders can help countries to put in place adequate health policies. The WHO guidelines aim to help WHO Member States and their partners to make evidence-informed decisions on appropriate actions in their efforts to lower iron deficiency and improve the health and quality of life of individuals and populations. title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia.
text: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here, we generated a single-cell multi-omic atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical human donors. This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis-regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia. Integration with matched MERFISH spatial transcriptomics further uncovered regional heterogeneity in epigenomic and transcriptional programs. Finally, we used this atlas to interpret noncoding risk variants associated with neuropsychiatric disorders and to construct a deep-learning model that predicts gene regulatory activities and variant effects. Together, this work provides a multimodal regulatory framework for understanding human basal ganglia organization, evolution, and disease genetics.

title: A single-cell lung cancer atlas reveals cellular and molecular drivers of metastasis and clinical outcome.
text: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, characterized by extensive cellular and molecular heterogeneity. Here, to capture this complexity, we present LuCaS+, a multicenter single-cell RNA sequencing atlas comprising over 2.5 million nuclei from 454 clinically annotated patients with NSCLC with long-term follow-up. LuCaS+ consists of a discovery dataset (Berlin and Cologne, 364 patients) and an independent validation dataset (Munich, 90 patients). Leveraging this dataset, we identified tumor subpopulations with high metastatic potential associated with oncogenic signaling, immune evasion and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. In early-stage adenocarcinoma (lung adenocarcinoma), these cells showed strong prognostic value. Integrating tumor and microenvironmental cell profiles improved survival prediction across all stages, identifying distinct tumor-immune-stromal interaction patterns. These included monocyte- and fibroblast-driven inflammation (lung adenocarcinoma), VEGF-TGFβ-mediated angiogenic feedback loops (lung squamous cell carcinoma) and immune-permissive niches promoting antitumor immunity. LuCaS+ offers a clinically anchored single-cell resource to enable personalized, biology-driven therapies in NSCLC.

title: Molecular Biomarkers and Biosensing Innovations for the Early Diagnosis of Ankylosing Spondylitis: From Molecular Mechanisms to Precision Diagnostics.
text: Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic immune-mediated, inflammatory spondyloarthropathy in which delayed diagnosis remains a major clinical challenge, particularly during the early stages when definitive structural radiographic changes may be absent. Although HLA-B27 represents the most potent genetic association with ankylosing spondylitis, its incomplete penetrance and variability limit its use as a single diagnostic biomarker. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms underlying HLA-B27-associated disease, evaluates circulating and molecular biomarkers according to their demonstrated clinical roles and assesses the current development of biosensing technologies for their detection. Biomarkers including IL-17, IL-13, TNF-α, MMP-3, calprotectin, microRNAs, and anti-CD74 antibodies reflect complementary aspects of inflammation, immune dysregulation and tissue remodelling; however, their biological association with the disease should not be compared with validated early diagnostic performance. Emerging optical and electrochemical biosensing platforms demonstrate promising analytical sensitivity and potential for rapid and minimally invasive detection. However, much of the available biosensor research remains at the level of analytical feasibility or biomarker detection, with limited evidence demonstrating discrimination of ankylosing spondylitis from clinical controls and very limited independent clinical validation. Major translational barriers include biomarker heterogeneity, sensor standardisation, and clinical testing. Future development should focus on clinically validated multi-biomarker biosensor systems, nanomaterial-enhanced detection and machine learning-assisted analysis. Collectively, the combination of molecular biomarker research and next-generation biosensing technology can elevate diagnostic accuracy, providing early intervention and precision medicine strategies for disease assessment.

title: Myeloid subpopulations correlate with responsiveness to therapy in a prospective, longitudinal study on RA patients
text: BackgroundRheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease associated with the destruction of cartilage and bone, increased risk of cardiovascular disease and a higher mortality rate. Despite the many therapies that exist for RA, there is little information to guide selection of the most effective treatment for an individual patient. Ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies have created an opportunity to investigate the target tissue. While a number of studies have characterized the stromal and immune cell populations using single-cell technology on synovial biopsy samples, here we performed a longitudinal study, where we collected comprehensive clinical data over a one-year period on each patient in the process of changing their therapy. MethodsSamples from minimally invasive, ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies were collected from RA patients at baseline prior to start of a new therapy and 4-6-week follow-up under IRB-approved protocols with informed consent. Comprehensive clinical data from each appointment were recorded into a shared REDCap database. Failure to respond to therapy was based on clinical disease activity index (CDAI) for RA after 12-18 weeks post therapy. Biopsied samples were dissociated, enriched for CD45 or CD45CD11b cells, and processed on the 10X Genomics Chromium platform to generate libraries for single-cell RNA sequencing with cell-surface protein detection (CITE-seq). Spatial transcriptomics were performed on formalin-fixed paraffin embedded sections analyzed with 10X Xenium and NanoString CosMx. ResultsWe performed CITE-seq analysis on [~]38,000 CD45+ synovial cells isolated from 17 patients who failed a conventional or biologic DMARD and planned to change therapy. We then subclustered on the myeloid population to reveal 12 myeloid subpopulations that consist of macrophages (n = 8), Osteoclast-like cells, DCs (n = 2) and proliferating cells. The proportion of cDCs was significantly higher in responders, while the proportion of macrophages was significantly lower in responders. The proportion of ISG15+and THBS1+macrophages were enriched in the non-responder patients. Spatial transcriptomics revealed that ISG15+ macrophages were preferentially localized to the synovial lining, while the THBS1+ macrophages are likely interacting with lymphoid cells within the sublining tissue. ConclusionsThese data are among the first to prospectively profile macrophage populations as predictors of response to therapy. Future studies are required to verify whether myeloid subpopulation associations hold across specific therapies.

title: Understanding the control of perpetual flowering and continuous runnering in strawberry
text: Consumer demand for year-round strawberry fruit has increased the need to extend the cropping season. Perpetual flowering cultivars, which produce fruit continuously throughout the growing season, offer a promising solution. However, these cultivars typically exhibit reduced runner production, due to a genetic trade-off between flowering and runnering, presenting challenges for propagation and breeding efforts. Additionally, limited understanding of the mechanisms controlling these traits in the cultivated strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) has hindered the application of advanced breeding or crop improvement tools. This PhD work aimed to better understand the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying perpetual flowering and continuous runnering in strawberry, to contribute to the development of perpetual flowering cultivars with extended fruiting periods and improved propagation potential. In this thesis the control of perpetual flowering was explored by functionally studying key f lowering genes TFL1 and FT1 in F. x ananassa seasonal flowering cultivar ‘Malling Centenary’ and perpetual flowering cultivar ‘Calypso’ using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing and phenotyping. FaTFL1 mutant lines exhibited early flowering and reduced runner production under long day conditions, validating its role as a floral repressor and demonstrating the regulatory link between these traits. FaFT1 mutant lines presented alteration in floral and fruit morphology suggesting its role in floral development. Furthermore, the genetic regulation of the trade-off between flowering and runnering was studied through genotyping-by-sequencing based QTL mapping using a woodland strawberry (Fragaria vesca) F₂ mapping population developed from a cross between an ecotype from Spain with continuous runnering habit and an accession from Iceland with a “standard” runnering habit. Two additive QTLs associated with continuous runnering were identified using interval mapping. The most significant QTL was narrowed and validated using cleave amplified polymorphic sequences (CAPS) for genotyping in a second validation population. Candidate genes associated with dormancy and axillary bud outgrowth were identified in both QTLs. Gene expression analysis showed a significant downregulation of two candidate genes in continuous runnering individuals supporting their role in the control of this trait. Finally, the functional role of the two main candidate genes for continuous runnering was explored through CRISPR/Cas9 targeted mutagenesis in F. vesca. Two mutant lines for one of the main candidate genes were obtained, however the editing efficiency was very low and consequently this part of the study was not pursued to completion. The work developed within this thesis provides valuable insight into the mechanisms controlling perpetual flowering and the developmental trade-off between generative and vegetative reproduction that could inform future crop improvement strategies.

title: Het opbouwen van ruimtelijke en single-cell transcriptomische atlassen om astrocytenheterogeniteit en -functie in gezondheid en ziekte te ontrafelen
text: Astrocytes comprise one of the major classes of glial cells in the mammalian brain and are essential for central nervous system (CNS) development and function. These cells contribute to diverse processes, including synapse formation, maintenance of synaptic homeostasis through the control of extracellular K+ levels and neurotransmitter clearance, modulation of synaptic transmission, formation and maintenance of the blood-brain barrier, control of cerebral blood flow, and immune responses. Yet,compared with their neuronal counterparts, their diversity and functional specialization remain incompletely understood. Increasing evidence supports the existence of a high degree of astrocyte heterogeneity throughout the CNS, both across and within brain regions, during development, and in injury and disease contexts. Importantly, recent advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics (ST) now enable the exploration of astrocyte heterogeneity with unprecedented depth and resolution. Using state-of-the-art single-cell and ST approaches, the overall aim of this project is to uncover different aspects of astrocyte diversity, from molecular heterogeneity in the healthy mouse brain across development and adulthood to heterogenous astrocyte responses in disease. Recent single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing studies have profiled millions of cells across the mouse brain. However, substantial technical differences between these methods have resulted in the identification of varying numbers of astrocyte populations and the use of distinct nomenclatures, making the alignment of findings across studies challenging. To address this, I established a unified atlas of adult mouse astrocytes by harmonizing multiple single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets into a unified reference framework. This work identified seven major populations and 37 subpopulations that vary in abundance across distinct brain regions and are characterized by specific molecular gene signatures. These findings provide a foundation for the future development of tools to target defined astrocyte populations and manipulate their function. This project further demonstrates how ST can be used to characterize the expression of particularly challenging transcripts, such as clustered protocadherins (cPcdh), which share highly similar sequences. Using a highly sensitive ST approach with subcellular resolution, I generated an atlas of postnatal mouse visual cortical development that enabled the detection of distinct cPcdh transcripts. Particularly, I show that α-cPcdhs are mainly enriched in neurons, whereas γ-cPcdhs are enriched in both neurons and astrocytes, with population-specific enrichment across astrocyte subpopulations. These findings support the idea that different populations of astrocytes may not equally participate in synapse formation and function, with potential implications for neurodevelopmental conditions such as Trisomy 21. Finally, this project extends the study of astrocyte molecular heterogeneity to human disease by generating single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic atlases of the substantia nigra pars compacta from donors with Parkinson's disease (PD) and control donors. Neurodegenerative conditions such as PD have traditionally been considered primary neuronal disorders. However, the contribution of non-neuronal populations in disease pathogenesis and progression remains poorly understood and is increasingly being recognized. Using single-nucleus and ST, I assessed cell-type-specific dysfunction in PD and found that PD is a multicellular disorder. These results support the view that glial cells, including astrocytes, adopt heterogenous molecular states that likely reflect different degrees of vulnerability or resilience in relation to the surrounding diseased environment.
